title: Coastal Surf Shop: purchases, sales, posting and the worksheet
participant_role: Accountant at the accounting firm that serves COASTAL SURF SHOP
judge_role: Owner of COASTAL SURF SHOP, who is training a new bookkeeper and wants a clear example to follow

difficulty.rationale: Merchandising entries with a purchase discount, posting and worksheet; basic cycle skills.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of an accountant at the accounting firm that serves COASTAL SURF SHOP. The owner (judge) of COASTAL SURF SHOP has hired a new part-time bookkeeper and has asked you to prepare a clear example the bookkeeper can follow.

COASTAL SURF SHOP sells surfboards, wetsuits and accessories. The shop uses a perpetual inventory system, so the Merchandise Inventory account is updated every time goods are bought, returned or sold, and the cost of each sale is recorded at the same time as the sale.

The owner (judge) has written these directions for the new bookkeeper: "Use the source documents to record every purchase and sale in the general journal. Post each entry to the ledger the same day. At the end of the month, use the worksheet to prepare the financial statements." The bookkeeper has asked for an example that shows every step.

At the beginning of the week, the shop had the following account balances: Cash $20,000; Merchandise Inventory $10,000; Accounts Payable $0.

[This week's transactions: see exhibits]

The owner (judge) wants the example to be accurate and easy to follow so the new bookkeeper can use it as a model for every week that follows.

You must:
- Explain the documents used for purchases and sales and the three-way match
- Journalize the five transactions
- Post the entries to the Merchandise Inventory, Accounts Payable and Cash ledger accounts and find each balance
- Explain the purpose and columns of a worksheet and where these balances go

You will present your recommendations to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's office at the shop. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your recommendations and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Explain the documents used for purchases and sales and the three-way match
Post the entries to the Merchandise Inventory, Accounts Payable and Cash ledger accounts and find each balance
Explain the purpose and columns of a worksheet and where these balances go

exhibits.title: This week's transactions
rows: Purchased surfboards on account from Wave Supply Co., $4,000, terms 2/10, n/30
Purchase order, receiving report and vendor invoice (all three agree)
Returned damaged surfboards to Wave Supply Co., $400
Debit memo sent to the vendor
Paid Wave Supply Co. the full amount owed, within the discount period
Sold merchandise on account, $3,000; cost of the merchandise sold $1,800
Cash sale, $1,200; cost of the merchandise sold $700

performance_indicators: Post journal entries to general ledger accounts
Apply written directions to achieve tasks

pi_links.text: Post journal entries to general ledger accounts
Apply written directions to achieve tasks

century_skills: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking
Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems
Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity
judge_questions: Why do we record the discount as a reduction of inventory instead of income?
Our new bookkeeper wants to skip posting and just use the journal. What's wrong with that?

solution.overview: A strong answer explains the purchase and sales documents and the three-way match, journalizes all five transactions under the perpetual system (including a $72 purchase discount and paired sale and cost entries) and posts them to reach ending balances of Merchandise Inventory $11,028, Accounts Payable $0 and Cash $17,672. The presenter shows sales of $4,200, cost of goods sold of $2,500 and gross profit of $1,700, then explains the ten-column worksheet and where each balance goes.

answer: Purchase requisition: an internal request for goods; purchase order: the shop's official order sent to the vendor
Receiving report: lists what actually arrived; vendor invoice: the bill showing the amount and terms
Three-way match: pay only when the purchase order, receiving report and invoice agree on items, quantities and prices
Sales invoice is the source document for a sale on account; a sales receipt is the source document for a cash sale
A debit memo documents the return and reduces what the shop owes the vendor
(a) Inventory and Accounts Payable each increase by $4,000
(b) The return reduces both Accounts Payable and Inventory by $400
(c) Amount owed 4,000 minus 400 = $3,600; discount 2% x 3,600 = $72; cash paid $3,528
(d) and (e) each need two entries: the sale at selling price and the cost of goods sold at cost
Sales $4,200 minus cost of goods sold $2,500 = gross profit $1,700
Posting copies each debit and credit from the journal to its ledger account, with the date and journal page reference
Merchandise Inventory: 10,000 + 4,000 minus 400 minus 72 minus 1,800 minus 700 = $11,028 debit
Accounts Payable: 4,000 minus 400 minus 3,600 = $0
The ledger shows the current balance of each account, which the journal alone cannot
A worksheet is an internal working paper that organizes the trial balance and adjustments; it is not a formal financial statement
The ten-column worksheet has debit and credit columns for the trial balance, adjustments, adjusted trial balance, income statement and balance sheet
Cash, Accounts Receivable, Merchandise Inventory and Accounts Payable go to the balance sheet columns
Sales and Cost of Goods Sold go to the income statement columns
The difference between the income statement columns is net income, which is carried to the balance sheet columns so they balance

journal_entries.description: (a) Purchased surfboards on account, terms 2/10, n/30
(b) Returned damaged surfboards to the vendor
(c) Paid the vendor within the discount period
(d) Recorded the cost of the merchandise sold on account
(e) Recorded the cost of the merchandise sold for cash

judge_question_answers.question: Why do we record the discount as a reduction of inventory instead of income?
answer: Under a perpetual system, inventory is recorded at what the goods actually cost
The boards really cost $3,528 net ($3,600 less the $72 discount), so inventory should show that cost
A discount is a lower purchase price, not revenue earned from customers
The saving shows up later as lower cost of goods sold, which raises gross profit when the boards are sold

judge_question_answers.question: Our new bookkeeper wants to skip posting and just use the journal. What's wrong with that?
answer: The journal lists transactions by date, but it does not show the balance of any one account
Without posting, no one can tell how much cash the shop has or what it owes a vendor
The trial balance and the worksheet are built from ledger balances, so statements could not be prepared
Following the written directions keeps the records consistent; software posts automatically, but the bookkeeper must still understand the process

key_concepts.definition: An inventory system that updates Merchandise Inventory and Cost of Goods Sold every time goods are bought, returned or sold.
The buyer's official written order to a vendor listing items, quantities and prices.
A document prepared when goods arrive that lists what was actually received.
Comparing the purchase order, receiving report and vendor invoice before paying, to make sure the shop pays only for goods ordered and received.
A 2% discount if the invoice is paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days. In a perpetual system it reduces inventory.
Goods sent back to the vendor, which reduces both Accounts Payable and Merchandise Inventory.
Source documents for sales: an invoice for a sale on account and a receipt for a cash sale.
The cost of the merchandise sold during the period. Gross profit = sales minus cost of goods sold.
Transferring each debit and credit from the journal to the correct general ledger account.
The collection of all accounts, each showing its increases, decreases and current balance.
A ten-column working paper used to organize the trial balance and adjustments and to prepare the financial statements. It is not a formal statement.

notes: State level because the student must handle a return, a purchase discount and paired sale and cost entries under a perpetual system, then post and explain the worksheet. Watch for students who take the discount on $4,000 instead of $3,600, who forget the cost of goods sold entries, or who call the worksheet a financial statement.

criteria.exceeds: Explains the purchase order, receiving report and vendor invoice and the three-way match, then records the $4,000 purchase (debit Merchandise Inventory, credit Accounts Payable), the $400 return with a debit memo, and the payment (debit Accounts Payable $3,600, credit Cash $3,528, credit Merchandise Inventory $72), explaining that the 2% discount applies to $3,600 after the return.
criteria.meets: Records the purchase, return and payment correctly, including the $72 discount credited to Merchandise Inventory and cash paid of $3,528.
criteria.below: Records the purchase and return but figures the discount on $4,000 ($80), credits a Purchase Discounts income account, or cannot explain the three-way match.
criteria.little: Does not journalize the purchase transactions, or the entries use unrelated accounts.

criteria.exceeds: Records both sales with paired entries under the perpetual system (debit Accounts Receivable $3,000, credit Sales $3,000 with debit Cost of Goods Sold $1,800, credit Merchandise Inventory $1,800; debit Cash $1,200, credit Sales $1,200 with debit Cost of Goods Sold $700, credit Merchandise Inventory $700), names the sales invoice and sales receipt, and shows gross profit of $1,700 ($4,200 minus $2,500).
criteria.meets: Records both sales at selling price and both cost of goods sold entries at cost, reaching sales of $4,200 and cost of goods sold of $2,500.
criteria.below: Records the sales revenue but forgets the cost of goods sold entries, or records the sales at cost.
criteria.little: Does not record the sales, or the entries are unrelated to the exhibit.

items.label: Post journal entries to general ledger accounts

criteria.exceeds: Explains that posting copies each debit and credit to its ledger account with the date and journal page reference, and walks through each running balance to reach Merchandise Inventory $11,028 debit, Accounts Payable $0 and Cash $17,672 debit.
criteria.meets: Posts the entries and reaches the correct ending balances: Merchandise Inventory $11,028, Accounts Payable $0 and Cash $17,672.
criteria.below: Posts most entries but reaches a wrong balance, for example leaving out the $72 discount or the cost of goods sold reductions in Merchandise Inventory.
criteria.little: Does not post the entries or find any account balances.

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the worksheet is an internal working paper, not a financial statement, describes the ten columns (trial balance, adjustments, adjusted trial balance, income statement and balance sheet, each debit and credit), places Cash, Accounts Receivable, Merchandise Inventory and Accounts Payable in the balance sheet columns and Sales and Cost of Goods Sold in the income statement columns, and shows net income carried over so the balance sheet columns balance.
criteria.meets: Describes the worksheet's purpose and its column sections and correctly says which balances go to the income statement and balance sheet columns.
criteria.below: Calls the worksheet a financial statement, or places accounts in the wrong columns.
criteria.little: Does not explain the worksheet or where the balances go.

items.label: Apply written directions to achieve tasks

criteria.exceeds: Follows the owner's written directions step by step (source documents, general journal, same day posting, worksheet) and turns them into a clear model the new bookkeeper can repeat every week.
criteria.meets: Completes each step the owner's directions require, in the correct order, using the source documents in the exhibit.
criteria.below: Skips a required step such as posting or the worksheet, or does the steps out of order.
criteria.little: Ignores the written directions or completes few of the required steps.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Shows how each transaction flows from source document to journal to ledger to worksheet, and why the return must come before the discount is figured on $3,600.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit to the entries and balances.
criteria.below: Reaches some answers without showing the reasoning, or misses how one step affects the next.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Handles the tricky items correctly (return, discount on the net amount, paired sale and cost entries) and suggests checks the bookkeeper can use, such as confirming Accounts Payable returns to $0.
criteria.meets: Solves the discount and perpetual inventory entries correctly.
criteria.below: Solves some items but makes errors on the discount or cost of goods sold.
criteria.little: Does not solve the key problems in the transactions.

criteria.exceeds: Explains every step in plain language a new part-time bookkeeper could follow, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the documents, entries, postings and worksheet clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses T accounts, a running balance table or a simple flow diagram that makes the example easy to reuse each week, and adds a useful idea such as a checklist for the three-way match.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the example easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: under a perpetual system the boards really cost $3,528 net, so the $72 discount lowers inventory cost rather than being revenue and later shows up as lower cost of goods sold; and skipping posting means no one can see account balances such as cash or what is owed, and the trial balance and worksheet cannot be built without the ledger.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that a discount lowers the cost of inventory and that the ledger is needed to know account balances.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without connecting to the $72 discount or the ledger balances.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or agrees that the discount is income or that posting can be skipped.

key_points: Three-way match: pay only when the purchase order, receiving report and vendor invoice agree
Payment: amount owed 4,000 minus 400 = $3,600; discount 2% x 3,600 = $72; cash paid $3,528
Payment entry: debit Accounts Payable $3,600, credit Cash $3,528, credit Merchandise Inventory $72
Each sale needs two entries: the sale at selling price and Cost of Goods Sold at cost ($1,800 and $700)
Sales $4,200 minus cost of goods sold $2,500 = gross profit $1,700
Ending balances: Merchandise Inventory $11,028 debit, Accounts Payable $0, Cash $17,672 debit

The ten-column worksheet is an internal working paper, not a financial statement; Sales and Cost of Goods Sold go to the income statement columns and asset and liability accounts go to the balance sheet columns
